compare_blocks.title: The key difference

compare_blocks.body:
The premise is aligned conditions: the same volunteer team, the same three-day holiday, the same post requirements, the same list of twelve people. If one is the team lead and the other only helps out, role will cover both columns.

Both types can use the other's approach: ESFJ will also calculate how many people each day needs, and INTP will also ask whose family has something on; the table records only which basis is taken first more often, not who moves first.

compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
Imagine two volunteers who both sign up to help with a holiday duty rota, holding the same list of twelve people's availability, the same post requirements and the same three days off. Both are willing to come; the difference is not who is more reliable, but which kind of basis each takes first once they have the list.

Their codes differ on E/I, S/N, T/F and J/P. The model orders Fe, Si, Ne and Ti differently for each. Both volunteers can follow the same procedure and get the job done.

The four axes are read separately. On sourcing, one more often trusts observable facts and past experience, the other notices connections and possibilities not yet in view; on judging, one more often brings people's circumstances and the effect on relationships into the weighing, the other asks first whether a standard can be applied consistently; on outward stance, one more often settles the arrangement, the other keeps options until new information arrives; on the direction of attention, one more often turns to the people and the occasion present, the other withdraws into their own reasoning. The four cannot substitute for each other, and none can be replaced by the order of actions.

### The same rota: what each may check first

In this fictional example, a volunteer needs to swap shifts on the second day of the holiday because their child is ill. Both face the same situation: the post has to be covered that day, the team lead has to be told, and a record has to be left.

One way to weigh the swap is to consider the people affected. Would a volunteer who took the shift have to work two days in a row? How much flexibility does the parent have? These questions illustrate the Feeling side of T/F.

Another way is to check whether the same criteria for approving an exception would hold if someone else requested a swap under the same conditions. That illustrates the Thinking side of T/F. Either volunteer could use both criteria.

Each consideration has a cost. Talking only about the human arrangements easily turns "whoever is accommodating covers more" into a custom; talking only about clauses easily leaves someone in a hurry feeling unheard. The cost is not about preference but about who owns the rota that day and whether the team has written rules.

The basis is not who replies first in the group, how many calls someone makes, or how the notes column is filled in — the note format usually follows the team's record-keeping rules. What discriminates better is the reason: why an exception is allowed this time, under what conditions it would not be, and whether another person asking would get the same answer.

Keep the counterexamples. INTP may quietly leave someone an exception and say only "let it go this time" in private; someone who argues from the rule also weighs the specific situation. ESFJ may also hold up the hours sheet and point out "three people served five times this month and two served none"; valuing relationships is not the same as not doing the arithmetic.

A workable check: each writes one line — "what most needs confirming about this swap" — and then they compare. If both write "who covers it", the disagreement is mainly about the human arrangement; if one writes "who covers it" and the other "does this kind of exception count in future", the boundary of the rule has to be discussed before the person is chosen. Both mentioning "the swap" does not mean the disagreement is only about handling: one may be worried about a gap that day, the other about long-term fairness, or about information not being handed over — those three have to be separated first.

### Why the four function names are identical but the order is reversed

In the common four-function notation used here, ESFJ is Fe–Si–Ne–Ti and INTP is Ti–Ne–Si–Fe, and the two are exact reverses: read ESFJ's arrangement from the bottom up and you get INTP's, with first and last swapped, the middle two swapped, and all four names present.

This is only a labelling convention. The four positions are dominant, auxiliary, third and inferior; ESFJ's third process is Intuition, written here as Ne, and INTP's third is Sensing, written here as Si, but whether the third process should be labelled introverted or extraverted is not consistent across tables, some giving only the function name. When a version differs, check which table it cites; the disagreement does not change the first two positions and does not explain how early someone speaks.

A position describes emphasis in preference, not proficiency and not an energy scale. In this framework the dominant position describes the information-processing or judging process called on first more often, and does not predict the difficulty of a specific task: an ESFJ who has built rotas for years may write the rules in more detail than anyone, and an INTP used to organising events may look after a roomful of feelings very well. Both base descriptions are the [ESFJ profile](/en/personality/esfj) and the [INTP profile](/en/personality/intp).
compare_blocks.title: Why they are easily confused

compare_blocks.body:
Scope note: the two passages below are fictional, covering communication and the organisation of information only, with no handling judgement; how a rota or a gathering is settled belongs to the organisers and the people involved, and type does not enter the division of work.

When the two work together, friction tends to appear when one is still in private messages and the other has already sent the rules out. It is rarely about who is right, but about which kind of information each handles first.

### Twelve people, three days, four posts a day

(Fictional scene.) Twelve people, three days, four posts a day, and an old rule that anyone on two consecutive days is not scheduled on the third. One more often runs a round of private messages first: who is going home, who is revising for an exam, who is not comfortable working with whom; these get written down and turned into a version most people can accept. The other more often writes the constraints as clauses first: four people a day, no shift over four hours, how a swap is recorded, who confirms an exception; then posts the empty slots and lets people fill them.

Private messages alone produce a rota that looks thoughtful and does not survive a question — why does she get two days off and I work two in a row; clauses alone produce a rota that looks fair and may schedule the person who most needs rest on the busiest day. Each approach has a blind spot, and the blind spot comes from the information taken, not from a ranking of types.

A workable combination is not divided by type: whoever knows the post constraints drafts the rules, whoever deals with members day to day collects the adjustment needs, exceptions are confirmed by the team lead or owner, and changes go into one record. Who does which part follows experience and duty, not four letters.

### A reunion of old classmates: invite the one who fell out with the class?

(Fictional scene.) A first reunion in ten years, and the class group starts a sign-up list. Someone mentions the classmate who fell out with the class president, and the mood freezes. One more often asks a few people privately first: will he come, will it be awkward if he does, would not inviting him hurt more; what comes first is how to seat both of them at the table. The other more often asks what the gathering is for: if it is catching up, coming or not changes nothing; if the point is to settle what happened, that should be a separate conversation, not dinner.

The one protecting the occasion fears a meal turning into a confrontation; the one asking about the purpose fears an evening where nobody says anything true. Both concerns hold, and they point at different risks.

The counterexamples are clear too. INTP may volunteer "I will ask him" so the organiser is not put on the spot; the offer shows willingness to help in that situation but cannot establish which process is involved. ESFJ may also say outright "we cannot smooth this over, he needs to know that sentence hurt"; valuing the relationship is not the same as avoiding disagreement, and not the same as papering over it.

One method worth trying: one person meets the classmate alone for tea first and asks whether he wants to come; no reconciliation segment is built into the evening. Split one large matter into two small ones and both sides find it easier to accept. Who makes the approach depends on who knows him better and who can raise it more easily.
compare_blocks.title: Illustrative scenarios

compare_blocks.body:
Do not read ESFJ's warmth as people-pleasing. Remembering who has served how many times and whose family has something on may be to make the rota defensible, or simply a habit of keeping people's situations in mind; the motive cannot be read off a type.

Do not read INTP's calm as coldness. Putting the rules first may come from having seen the mess that "arranging by feel" produces; asked to sit and listen, they can listen for a long time.

Nor judge by "can they build a spreadsheet". A spreadsheet is a tool, and both types can make a good one; whether the notes column holds remarks or clauses depends more on the team's record-keeping rules and on who will read the sheet.

One more: "all four letters differ" does not mean "nothing in common". This pair has exactly the same four function names and differs in the seating; reading only the letters suggests no common language, and reading only the function names suggests the two are the same.

(Fictional scene.) A first reunion in ten years, and the class group starts a sign-up list. Someone mentions the classmate who fell out with the class president, and the mood freezes. One more often asks a few people privately first: will he come, will it be awkward if he does, would not inviting him hurt more; what comes first is how to seat both of them at the table. The other more often asks what the gathering is for: if it is catching up, coming or not changes nothing; if the point is to settle what happened, that should be a separate conversation, not dinner.

faq_blocks.answer:
Both types can care about people and use rules. This shorthand only touches on T/F: how much weight a decision gives to people and values or to criteria applied consistently. The two types also differ on E/I, S/N and J/P.

What is worth pursuing is the reason. Both may allow one exception: ESFJ perhaps because this person genuinely has no room to move right now, INTP perhaps because the clause left that door open; the reverse also holds. faq_blocks.question: Can the difference be summarised as "cares about people" versus "argues from rules"?

faq_blocks.answer:
In the common four-function notation used here, the difference is the order of the functions: ESFJ is Fe–Si–Ne–Ti, INTP is Ti–Ne–Si–Fe, exact reverses, with Feeling dominant on one side and Thinking on the other.

The steadier method is to return to the four axes: whether sourcing trusts facts and experience or pattern and possibility (S/N), whether judgement weighs a consistent standard or people and values (T/F), whether the outward step settles an arrangement or keeps options (J/P), and whether attention turns outward or inward more often (E/I). A position describes preference emphasis only, predicts neither who does what first nor who is better at any part.
faq_blocks.question: The four functions are identical, so how are ESFJ and INTP distinguished?

faq_blocks.answer:
They are counterexamples to a behavioural stereotype, not a disproof of a type. Looking after people and counting hours are capacities both types have; whether they do it, and how well, depends on experience, duty and whether there is capacity at the time.

Say both kinds of effort out loud first, then discuss the practice. One is shielding people from trouble, the other is giving the work a rule; unsaid, each reads the other's approach as not caring.

body: Imagine two volunteers who both sign up to help with a holiday duty rota, holding the same list of twelve people's availability, the same post requirements and the same three days off. Both are willing to come; the difference is not who is more reliable, but which kind of basis each takes first once they have the list.
Their codes differ on E/I, S/N, T/F and J/P. The model orders Fe, Si, Ne and Ti differently for each. Both volunteers can follow the same procedure and get the job done.

The four axes are read separately. On sourcing, one more often trusts observable facts and past experience, the other notices connections and possibilities not yet in view; on judging, one more often brings people's circumstances and the effect on relationships into the weighing, the other asks first whether a standard can be applied consistently; on outward stance, one more often settles the arrangement, the other keeps options until new information arrives; on the direction of attention, one more often turns to the people and the occasion present, the other withdraws into their own reasoning. The four cannot substitute for each other, and none can be replaced by the order of actions.
### The same rota: what each may check first

In this fictional example, a volunteer needs to swap shifts on the second day of the holiday because their child is ill. Both face the same situation: the post has to be covered that day, the team lead has to be told, and a record has to be left.

One way to weigh the swap is to consider the people affected. Would a volunteer who took the shift have to work two days in a row? How much flexibility does the parent have? These questions illustrate the Feeling side of T/F.

Another way is to check whether the same criteria for approving an exception would hold if someone else requested a swap under the same conditions. That illustrates the Thinking side of T/F. Either volunteer could use both criteria.

Each consideration has a cost. Talking only about the human arrangements easily turns "whoever is accommodating covers more" into a custom; talking only about clauses easily leaves someone in a hurry feeling unheard. The cost is not about preference but about who owns the rota that day and whether the team has written rules.

The basis is not who replies first in the group, how many calls someone makes, or how the notes column is filled in — the note format usually follows the team's record-keeping rules. What discriminates better is the reason: why an exception is allowed this time, under what conditions it would not be, and whether another person asking would get the same answer.

Keep the counterexamples. INTP may quietly leave someone an exception and say only "let it go this time" in private; someone who argues from the rule also weighs the specific situation. ESFJ may also hold up the hours sheet and point out "three people served five times this month and two served none"; valuing relationships is not the same as not doing the arithmetic.

A workable check: each writes one line — "what most needs confirming about this swap" — and then they compare. If both write "who covers it", the disagreement is mainly about the human arrangement; if one writes "who covers it" and the other "does this kind of exception count in future", the boundary of the rule has to be discussed before the person is chosen. Both mentioning "the swap" does not mean the disagreement is only about handling: one may be worried about a gap that day, the other about long-term fairness, or about information not being handed over — those three have to be separated first.
### Why the four function names are identical but the order is reversed

In the common four-function notation used here, ESFJ is Fe–Si–Ne–Ti and INTP is Ti–Ne–Si–Fe, and the two are exact reverses: read ESFJ's arrangement from the bottom up and you get INTP's, with first and last swapped, the middle two swapped, and all four names present.

This is only a labelling convention. The four positions are dominant, auxiliary, third and inferior; ESFJ's third process is Intuition, written here as Ne, and INTP's third is Sensing, written here as Si, but whether the third process should be labelled introverted or extraverted is not consistent across tables, some giving only the function name. When a version differs, check which table it cites; the disagreement does not change the first two positions and does not explain how early someone speaks.

A position describes emphasis in preference, not proficiency and not an energy scale. In this framework the dominant position describes the information-processing or judging process called on first more often, and does not predict the difficulty of a specific task: an ESFJ who has built rotas for years may write the rules in more detail than anyone, and an INTP used to organising events may look after a roomful of feelings very well. Both base descriptions are the [ESFJ profile](/en/personality/esfj) and the [INTP profile](/en/personality/intp).

comparison_public_projection_v1.summary:
ESFJ and INTP share no letter: ESFJ is E, S, F, J and INTP is I, N, T, P. All four preference letters differ. In the four-function notation used here, the same function labels appear in reverse order.

Each of the four axes says one thing, and none can be flattened into "one cares about people, one argues from rules":

- E/I: ESFJ's E turns attention and energy outward more often, onto the people and the occasion in front of them; INTP's I turns inward more often, onto their own ideas and reasoning. This describes direction, not social skill and not how much someone talks.
- S/N: ESFJ's S more often takes observable facts, concrete experience and what has already happened; INTP's N more often takes connections between pieces of information, patterns and possibilities not yet in view.
- T/F: ESFJ's F more often brings people, values and the effect on relationships into the weighing; INTP's T more often judges by impersonal criteria that can be applied consistently.
- J/P: ESFJ's J more often forms an arrangement and a conclusion outward; INTP's P more often keeps options and adjusts when new information arrives.

In the common four-function notation used here, ESFJ is Fe–Si–Ne–Ti and INTP is Ti–Ne–Si–Fe: the same four parts, in exactly opposite order. The attitude of the third process (Ne for ESFJ, Si for INTP) is labelled differently elsewhere, and this writing is a convention adopted here, not the Foundation's only version.

These are emphases in preference inside the model. They do not predict who does what first, which task someone is more practised at, how tired the work leaves them, or whether two people get along; the order of events on a rota is shaped more by the duty, the urgency, experience and the record-keeping rules.

sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
Imagine two volunteers who both sign up to help with a holiday duty rota, holding the same list of twelve people's availability, the same post requirements and the same three days off. Both are willing to come; the difference is not who is more reliable, but which kind of basis each takes first once they have the list.

Their codes differ on E/I, S/N, T/F and J/P. The model orders Fe, Si, Ne and Ti differently for each. Both volunteers can follow the same procedure and get the job done.

The four axes are read separately. On sourcing, one more often trusts observable facts and past experience, the other notices connections and possibilities not yet in view; on judging, one more often brings people's circumstances and the effect on relationships into the weighing, the other asks first whether a standard can be applied consistently; on outward stance, one more often settles the arrangement, the other keeps options until new information arrives; on the direction of attention, one more often turns to the people and the occasion present, the other withdraws into their own reasoning. The four cannot substitute for each other, and none can be replaced by the order of actions.

### The same rota: what each may check first

In this fictional example, a volunteer needs to swap shifts on the second day of the holiday because their child is ill. Both face the same situation: the post has to be covered that day, the team lead has to be told, and a record has to be left.

One way to weigh the swap is to consider the people affected. Would a volunteer who took the shift have to work two days in a row? How much flexibility does the parent have? These questions illustrate the Feeling side of T/F.

Another way is to check whether the same criteria for approving an exception would hold if someone else requested a swap under the same conditions. That illustrates the Thinking side of T/F. Either volunteer could use both criteria.

Each consideration has a cost. Talking only about the human arrangements easily turns "whoever is accommodating covers more" into a custom; talking only about clauses easily leaves someone in a hurry feeling unheard. The cost is not about preference but about who owns the rota that day and whether the team has written rules.

The basis is not who replies first in the group, how many calls someone makes, or how the notes column is filled in — the note format usually follows the team's record-keeping rules. What discriminates better is the reason: why an exception is allowed this time, under what conditions it would not be, and whether another person asking would get the same answer.

Keep the counterexamples. INTP may quietly leave someone an exception and say only "let it go this time" in private; someone who argues from the rule also weighs the specific situation. ESFJ may also hold up the hours sheet and point out "three people served five times this month and two served none"; valuing relationships is not the same as not doing the arithmetic.

A workable check: each writes one line — "what most needs confirming about this swap" — and then they compare. If both write "who covers it", the disagreement is mainly about the human arrangement; if one writes "who covers it" and the other "does this kind of exception count in future", the boundary of the rule has to be discussed before the person is chosen. Both mentioning "the swap" does not mean the disagreement is only about handling: one may be worried about a gap that day, the other about long-term fairness, or about information not being handed over — those three have to be separated first.

### Why the four function names are identical but the order is reversed

In the common four-function notation used here, ESFJ is Fe–Si–Ne–Ti and INTP is Ti–Ne–Si–Fe, and the two are exact reverses: read ESFJ's arrangement from the bottom up and you get INTP's, with first and last swapped, the middle two swapped, and all four names present.

This is only a labelling convention. The four positions are dominant, auxiliary, third and inferior; ESFJ's third process is Intuition, written here as Ne, and INTP's third is Sensing, written here as Si, but whether the third process should be labelled introverted or extraverted is not consistent across tables, some giving only the function name. When a version differs, check which table it cites; the disagreement does not change the first two positions and does not explain how early someone speaks.

A position describes emphasis in preference, not proficiency and not an energy scale. In this framework the dominant position describes the information-processing or judging process called on first more often, and does not predict the difficulty of a specific task: an ESFJ who has built rotas for years may write the rules in more detail than anyone, and an INTP used to organising events may look after a roomful of feelings very well. Both base descriptions are the [ESFJ profile](/en/personality/esfj) and the [INTP profile](/en/personality/intp).

sections.body_md:
The premise is aligned conditions: the same volunteer team, the same three-day holiday, the same post requirements, the same list of twelve people. If one is the team lead and the other only helps out, role will cover both columns.

Each row is written as "the basis each may attend to in the same event", and the last column names the axis the row mainly sits on. Both types can use the other's approach: ESFJ will also calculate how many people each day needs, and INTP will also ask whose family has something on; the table records only which basis is taken first more often, not who moves first.

| The same event (one team, one availability list, the same three days) | ESFJ: the basis more likely attended to | INTP: the basis more likely attended to | What this row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The list of twelve people arrives | Which shifts have confirmed availability and what happened when the same schedule was used before | Which patterns in availability suggest more than one way to cover the shifts | Information used, leaning S/N |
| Fitting your own three days in | May find it easier to understand the same availability through discussion with the group | May find it easier to understand the same availability by reflecting privately | Direction of attention and energy, leaning E/I |
| Someone needs a swap at short notice | What the swap loads onto the other person, and how urgent this person's situation is | Whether this fits the exception clause, and how it counts next time once recorded | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |
| Someone has not been scheduled at all | Weigh how being left off the rota affects the person and the people sharing the workload | Apply the same rotation criteria to the verified schedule and any proposed adjustment | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |
| Someone says it is unfair | Weigh what the same hours and conditions mean to those affected | Apply the same rule for fairness to everyone’s confirmed hours and conditions | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |
| The post-holiday review | May agree on a provisional rota using the same review findings | May keep several workable rota options open while new availability is confirmed | Outward stance, leaning J/P |

The differences in the table are not a scale of ability. An ESFJ who has led volunteer teams for years more often sets the rules from experience first, and an INTP who has just joined may ask everyone about their availability one by one. The same person also changes approach with duty, information and whether the team has written rules, so these rows cannot be used to classify.
sections.title: ESFJ and INTP in one minute

sections.body_md:
Scope note: the two passages below are fictional, covering communication and the organisation of information only, with no handling judgement; how a rota or a gathering is settled belongs to the organisers and the people involved, and type does not enter the division of work.

When the two work together, friction tends to appear when one is still in private messages and the other has already sent the rules out. It is rarely about who is right, but about which kind of information each handles first.

### Twelve people, three days, four posts a day

(Fictional scene.) Twelve people, three days, four posts a day, and an old rule that anyone on two consecutive days is not scheduled on the third. One more often runs a round of private messages first: who is going home, who is revising for an exam, who is not comfortable working with whom; these get written down and turned into a version most people can accept. The other more often writes the constraints as clauses first: four people a day, no shift over four hours, how a swap is recorded, who confirms an exception; then posts the empty slots and lets people fill them.

Private messages alone produce a rota that looks thoughtful and does not survive a question — why does she get two days off and I work two in a row; clauses alone produce a rota that looks fair and may schedule the person who most needs rest on the busiest day. Each approach has a blind spot, and the blind spot comes from the information taken, not from a ranking of types.

A workable combination is not divided by type: whoever knows the post constraints drafts the rules, whoever deals with members day to day collects the adjustment needs, exceptions are confirmed by the team lead or owner, and changes go into one record. Who does which part follows experience and duty, not four letters.

### A reunion of old classmates: invite the one who fell out with the class?

(Fictional scene.) A first reunion in ten years, and the class group starts a sign-up list. Someone mentions the classmate who fell out with the class president, and the mood freezes. One more often asks a few people privately first: will he come, will it be awkward if he does, would not inviting him hurt more; what comes first is how to seat both of them at the table. The other more often asks what the gathering is for: if it is catching up, coming or not changes nothing; if the point is to settle what happened, that should be a separate conversation, not dinner.

The one protecting the occasion fears a meal turning into a confrontation; the one asking about the purpose fears an evening where nobody says anything true. Both concerns hold, and they point at different risks.

The counterexamples are clear too. INTP may volunteer "I will ask him" so the organiser is not put on the spot; the offer shows willingness to help in that situation but cannot establish which process is involved. ESFJ may also say outright "we cannot smooth this over, he needs to know that sentence hurt"; valuing the relationship is not the same as avoiding disagreement, and not the same as papering over it.

One method worth trying: one person meets the classmate alone for tea first and asks whether he wants to come; no reconciliation segment is built into the evening. Split one large matter into two small ones and both sides find it easier to accept. Who makes the approach depends on who knows him better and who can raise it more easily.

sections.body_md:
Do not read ESFJ's warmth as people-pleasing. Remembering who has served how many times and whose family has something on may be to make the rota defensible, or simply a habit of keeping people's situations in mind; the motive cannot be read off a type.

Do not read INTP's calm as coldness. Putting the rules first may come from having seen the mess that "arranging by feel" produces; asked to sit and listen, they can listen for a long time.

Nor judge by "can they build a spreadsheet". A spreadsheet is a tool, and both types can make a good one; whether the notes column holds remarks or clauses depends more on the team's record-keeping rules and on who will read the sheet.

One more: "all four letters differ" does not mean "nothing in common". This pair has exactly the same four function names and differs in the seating; reading only the letters suggests no common language, and reading only the function names suggests the two are the same.
sections.title: ESFJ and INTP: avoiding misreads

sections.body_md:
When two results differ, check whether the same version was used and whether you answered from the same reference situation, then look at what you were doing at the time: had you just taken on something that required constant contact with people, or just been asked to design a process nobody had tested. Circumstances push answers to one side, and one score cannot establish a stable tendency.

A workable exercise: find a few recent occasions that required arranging other people — a duty rota, a trip, dividing up tasks — and write a few lines for each: your duty and constraints, which information you noticed, which standard you weighed it against, and whether a change of conditions would change the approach. Writing it down is to see your own way of weighing, not to classify, and no threshold of "how many times in the same direction counts" is set.

Counterexamples matter as much: if you used the other kind of basis in a similar situation, both approaches are within your range. These notes are not scored, do not assign a type, and a few weeks of trend cannot replace an interpretation of the assessment result.
sections.title: ESFJ and INTP: how to keep observing

items.answer:
Both types can care about people and use rules. This shorthand only touches on T/F: how much weight a decision gives to people and values or to criteria applied consistently. The two types also differ on E/I, S/N and J/P.

What is worth pursuing is the reason. Both may allow one exception: ESFJ perhaps because this person genuinely has no room to move right now, INTP perhaps because the clause left that door open; the reverse also holds. Asking "why is it allowed this time, and under what conditions would it not be" shows each person's weighing better than watching who speaks first.
items.question: Can the difference be summarised as "cares about people" versus "argues from rules"?

items.answer:
In the common four-function notation used here, the difference is the order of the functions: ESFJ is Fe–Si–Ne–Ti, INTP is Ti–Ne–Si–Fe, exact reverses, with Feeling dominant on one side and Thinking on the other.

The steadier method is to return to the four axes: whether sourcing trusts facts and experience or pattern and possibility (S/N), whether judgement weighs a consistent standard or people and values (T/F), whether the outward step settles an arrangement or keeps options (J/P), and whether attention turns outward or inward more often (E/I). A position describes preference emphasis only, predicts neither who does what first nor who is better at any part.
items.question: The four functions are identical, so how are ESFJ and INTP distinguished?

items.answer:
They are counterexamples to a behavioural stereotype, not a disproof of a type. Looking after people and counting hours are capacities both types have; whether they do it, and how well, depends on experience, duty and whether there is capacity at the time.

The basis is not whether it was done but the reason: did you adjust because this person's situation needed to be met, or because the original standard did not hold? That reason says more about the entry point than a single behaviour, but it too has to be read across comparable situations; one performance is not a criterion.
items.question: INTP also looks after people and ESFJ also counts hours — are those counterexamples?

items.answer:
Do not divide by type. Building the sheet needs two kinds of work: writing the rules clearly so the sheet survives questions, and collecting people's difficulties so the sheet is accepted. Either type can do either part.

In practice, divide by experience and duty: whoever knows the post constraints drafts the rules, whoever deals with members collects the adjustment needs, exceptions are confirmed by the owner, and every change goes into one record. If one person does it alone, they can run both passes themselves: write the rules, then ask of each one whether it corners somebody.
items.question: For a volunteer rota, who is better suited to build the sheet?

items.answer:
Say both kinds of effort out loud first, then discuss the practice. One is shielding people from trouble, the other is giving the work a rule; unsaid, each reads the other's approach as not caring.

Two sentences can be agreed: when an exception comes up, ask first "why is it allowed this time", then "under what conditions would it not be next time". One needs to be heard, the other needs the standard not to be changed quietly, and both can be satisfied at once; most misunderstanding comes from reading "did not do it my way" as "does not value me", not from type itself.
items.question: When one values consideration and the other values standards, how do they reduce misunderstanding?

items.answer:
Check whether the same version was used and whether you answered from the same reference situation, then whether the report gives dimension-level information. For a pair with no shared letters, look axis by axis at which letters are changing, rather than saying vaguely that you are "on a boundary".

If the report gives dimension scores, look at which axes sit near the boundary; sitting near one only suggests that label is sensitive to changes in your answers, and does not mean ESFJ and INTP both hold as complete types. Without dimension scores or scoring notes, do not infer a boundary, and no retest interval is prescribed; testing again later in another situation, the movement itself need not be treated as a contradiction.
